diagnostic_evidence.quote: when $\omega > 1$ is used (which is the case of interest in overrelaxation) it cannot be guaranteed that positive definite matrices are generated

issues.failure_explanation: The sentence asserts that for some neighborhood O of Y_* the iteration map S_omega is well defined as a map C_m x O -> C_m x C_n. For omega > 1 (the regime of interest) this is false: fixing any Y in O and taking X = t*I_m in C_m, the first component (1-omega)X + omega S_1(Y) has eigenvalues (1-omega)t + omega*lambda_i(S_1(Y)), which tend to -infinity as t grows, so the first component is not positive definite for large t and S_2 cannot be applied. The paper itself concedes this two sentences earlier ('it cannot be guaranteed that positive definite matrices are generated'), contradicting the claimed codomain C_m x C_n on the stated domain.

failure_location.quote: is well defined as a map from $\caC_m \times \mathcal O$ to $\caC_m \times \caC_n$ and allows to write a single step of~\eqref{eq: overrelaxation Euclidean} as

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the claim to what is used later: S_omega is well defined and smooth on some neighborhood of (X_*,Y_*) (and of each point of the orbit), not on all of C_m x O; this one-line domain restriction preserves every subsequent claim.
issues.overall_effect: The stated domain/codomain guarantee for the iteration map of Algorithm PD-OR is false as written. No labelled result depends on it: Lemma lem: equal derivatives and Theorem thm: local convergence only require well-definedness locally near the fixed point, where the map is indeed well defined (as the paper notes in the following sentence).
issues.title: Overrelaxation map claimed well-defined on all of C_m x O although PD output fails for omega > 1
issues.why_classification: A local restriction of the claimed domain (which the paper itself states immediately afterwards) fully repairs the claim; no argument, rate, or guarantee is lost, so the repair is short and local.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we set $n = 50$, $k = 55$, and generate an initial frame from the standard Gaussian distribution

issues.failure_explanation: The stated goal (||tilde x_i||_2 = n/k for all i, and sum_i tilde x_i tilde x_i^T = I_n) is internally inconsistent unless k = n: taking traces gives sum_i ||tilde x_i||^2 = k(n/k)^2 = n^2/k, which must equal tr(I_n) = n; the experiment uses k = 55, n = 50, where n^2/k = 45.45... != 50, so the stated problem has no solution. The claimed correspondence is also false: with an operator-scaling solution (l_i^2 ||R x_i||^2 = 1/k, sum_i l_i^2 R x_i x_i^T R^T = I_n/n), setting alpha_i = n l_i^2 gives ||tilde x_i||_2^2 = alpha_i^2 ||R x_i||^2 = n^2 l_i^4 / (k l_i^2) = n^2 l_i^2/k, which is not constant in i in general, and sum_i tilde x_i tilde x_i^T = n^2 sum_i l_i^4 R x_i x_i^T R^T != I_n. The consistent translation is alpha_i = sqrt(n) l_i together with the normalization ||tilde x_i||_2 = sqrt(n/k): then l_i^2||R x_i||^2 = n l_i^2 * (1/(k l_i^2)) = n/k and sum_i tilde x_i tilde x_i^T = n * (1/n) I = I, recovering the (correct) equivalence with Tyler's M-estimator.

failure_location.quote: So $P = R$ and $\alpha_i = n\ell_i^2$ yield a solution to frame scaling, and vice versa.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Fix the normalization constants in the translation: state the frame goal as ||tilde x_i||_2 = sqrt(n/k) (equivalently ||tilde x_i||_2^2 = n/k) with sum_i tilde x_i tilde x_i^T = I_n, and set alpha_i = sqrt(n) l_i; the equivalence proof then goes through verbatim.
issues.overall_effect: The formulation of the frame-scaling application and the claimed iff-equivalence with operator scaling (in both directions) are false as stated; the underlying experiments are unaffected because the algorithms solve the operator scaling system itself, not the misstated frame conditions.
issues.title: Stated frame-scaling normalization is infeasible and the correspondence alpha_i = n*ell_i^2 is wrong
issues.why_classification: A local correction of two normalization constants restores the (true) equivalence between frame scaling and operator scaling and every advertised application; no argument, rate, or experimental conclusion changes.

issues.failure_explanation: With A_t = L_t A R_t^T, X_t = L_t^T L_t, Y_t = R_t^T R_t one has sum_i A_{t,i}A_{t,i}^T - I_m/m = L_t (Phi(Y_t) - (1/m)X_t^{-1}) L_t^T = L_t grad_X f L_t^T and sum_i A_{t,i}^T A_{t,i} - I_n/n = R_t grad_Y f R_t^T, so err(A_t)^2 = ||L_t grad_X f L_t^T||_F^2 + ||R_t grad_Y f R_t^T||_F^2. The Frobenius norm is not invariant under congruence by general GL factors L_t, R_t, so err is the norm of a congruence-transformed gradient, not of the gradient itself. Counterexample: m = n = k = 1, A_1 = 1, L_t = 2, R_t = 1, so X_t = 4, Y_t = 1: err = |4-1|*sqrt(2) = 3*sqrt(2) ≈ 4.24, while ||grad f(4,1)|| = sqrt((1-1/4)^2 + (4-1)^2) = sqrt(153)/4 ≈ 3.09.

failure_location.quote: It turns out that this error equals the norm of the gradient of $f$ (see~\eqref{eq: cost function}). Therefore, we call it the gradient norm.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Weaken the claim to: err(A_t) is the Frobenius norm of the congruence-transformed gradient (L_t grad_X f L_t^T, R_t grad_Y f R_t^T) and vanishes exactly when the gradient of f vanishes; no experiment needs to be redone.
issues.overall_effect: The interpretation of the plotted error measure as the gradient norm of f is false; the two quantities do vanish simultaneously, so the convergence comparisons and the adaptive choice of omega are not invalidated, but the stated identity and the terminology are wrong.
issues.title: Claimed identity between the error measure and the gradient norm of f is false
issues.why_classification: The repair is a local rewording of one sentence; the error measure remains a valid, gradient-equivalent convergence measure, and no formal result, rate, or experimental guarantee depends on the exact equality.
